page_placements.theme: Suppressive attention heads, often working as populations, in other models and tasks
Training decides which heads carry suppressive roles and how strongly

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports experiments on in-context-learning brake heads, but does not test GPT-2 small L10H7 or the defined copy-suppression behavior. It mentions copy-suppression heads as an analogy for its brakes.
record.gate_note: The study's brake heads suppress the most recently seen label to counter recency in in-context learning. This is related to, but not a test of, suppressing a token predicted by earlier components because it already occurs in context. Those brake results are recorded as findings that fit none of the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study maps an in-context-learning circuit in Qwen3, SmolLM3 and Llama-3.2. It finds 'brake' heads that write against the most recently seen label to cancel the readers' recency bias. The authors call these negative heads 'like' copy-suppression heads, but only as an analogy. They never examine GPT-2 small L10H7. They do not test whether brakes suppress tokens that are both predicted upstream and present in context, and they do not analyse brake QK/OV circuits as copy suppression. There is no measure of calibration on the training distribution and no self-repair experiment. The brake results are a related construct (anti-recency label suppression), so they belong under fits_no_version rather than as a test of V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors describe brakes as negative heads analogous to negative name movers and copy-suppression heads. They give brakes the job of calibrating against recency in ICL label retrieval, and they make no claim about GPT-2 small L10H7 or copy suppression on the training distribution.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses activation patching, head ablations, steering, and head-population analyses on in-context-learning tasks in Qwen, SmolLM3, Llama, and other models. It does not reproduce the GPT-2 small L10H7 analysis or its loss-attribution measure.
record.method_sensitivity: Brake effects are reported to vary with model size, label type, and demonstration count; the brake population's summed effect at 8B is lower than at 4B.

fits_no_version.finding: In Qwen3-4B-Base, knocking out 24 brake heads on a fresh draw raises the margin by +1.39 [+0.88, +1.88], against +0.22 for random heads. With brakes removed, the model prefers whichever label came last.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A population of late attention heads in ICL writes against the most recently seen label, cancelling the readers' recency bias.

fits_no_version.finding: In Llama-3.2-3B, no single head moves the margin by more than 0.12. Yet the 24 census-ranked brakes knocked out jointly give +1.90 at 12 demonstrations and +0.57 at 6, against +0.12 and +0.16 for random sets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Anti-recency negative heads can exist as a population whose joint effect is large while single-head effects are negligible.

fits_no_version.finding: Across Qwen3 0.6B–8B, brake populations appear at every size: summed effects of +0.82, +1.21, +3.76 and +3.27, a non-monotone pattern. Brakes on word meaning rise monotonically (+1.73 to +4.03) with the flipped-label margin.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Negative heads that hold down label-word priors grow with model size and track the ability to follow flipped labels.

fits_no_version.finding: In Qwen3-4B instruct, unnamed heads in layers 16–27 hold down the word-meaning part of the margin by about 4.9 nats (about 2 in base). Many-shot LoRA left brake strength unchanged.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Post-training increases braking against label priors in the population around the retrieval circuit, while few-hundred-step fine-tuning does not change brake strength.

record.problems: The paper studies a different behavior and does not test the specified GPT-2 small head or the claim's loss contribution. Some aggregate brake-census values are sums of single-head effects rather than joint ablations.
record.rows_left_out: Other results about the in-context-learning circuit, including writers, readers, gates, and the key–value readout, are not recorded because they do not measure the copy-suppression behavior in the claim. The reported random-head comparisons are noted alongside the corresponding brake rows rather than given separate rows.

untested.parts: GPT-2 small L10H7 is never studied, and there is no training-distribution analysis of suppressing predicted, in-context tokens.
There is no QK/OV weight analysis of a copy-suppression head and no loss-attribution measure (e.g. 76.9%).
Calibration and overconfidence in naive copying are not measured. 'Calibrate against recency' refers to order effects in label retrieval, not probability calibration.
There are no upstream-copier ablations and no measurement of copy suppression's contribution to self-repair.

Brakes are only likened to negative name movers and copy-suppression heads. The paper does not test whether they implement the copy-suppression mechanism (attending to predicted, context-present tokens and negatively copying them).
There is no decomposition of self-repair into copy suppression versus LayerNorm or other components.

record.verdict_notes: The analogy to McDougall et al. appears in Section 7 and Related Work only. Table 4 lists SmolLM3 brakes as 'suppressors', with three named order carriers; this is unrecorded but also fits no version. The recency-cancellation behaviour is conceptually close to copy suppression of a context-present, being-copied token. A future version on 'negative heads in ICL suppress copied labels' could make this study relevant.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test GPT-2 small L10H7 or whether one head has the stated role across the training distribution.
No GPT-2 small L10H7 QK/OV-circuit analysis or measurement of its contribution to loss is reported.
The study does not test whether copy suppression improves calibration by reducing overconfidence in copying.
The study does not test copy suppression as self-repair after upstream copier ablation.

The paper compares its anti-recency brake heads to negative heads and copy-suppression heads, but does not test whether they perform the same copy-suppression behavior in GPT-2 small, IOI, or other models.
The study does not measure the contribution of copy suppression versus other mechanisms to self-repair.

relation.reason: Sections 7 and 13 explicitly compare brakes with copy-suppression heads; copy suppression is neither an experimental target nor a tool used by the study.

tranche.reason: The experiments establish ICL recency suppression, without testing identity with the copy-suppression role or the mechanisms and distributional claims in V1–V6.

source_check.notes: Observed states describe the reported knockout effects, not support for a claim version. Census rows r6–r13 are selection-dependent descriptive totals; r15 shows an observed knockout effect and a null training comparison.
